{{< include _arrange-kit.qmd >}}

The words say what happens. The music says **how it feels**, and a listener often believes the music over the words. If a sad line sits on bright,
busy music, the song sounds like it is lying; if the music slowly changes as the story does, the listener feels the story without being told.
This lesson shows five tools. Each example is the site's own band: press **▶ Play**, and use the buttons to switch players and versions.

**How to use the page.** The chords are the same four (C, G, Am, F) in most examples, so that you hear only the change being made.

## 1. Start small, finish big: dynamics and texture

A ballad rarely starts at full volume. It starts with the fewest players, often one chord instrument and the voice, and adds as the story gains weight:
bass in verse 2, drums in the chorus, everyone in the last chorus. Then often it takes everything away for one line.

Hear the same four chords with one player, then two, then the whole band. Press the **Who plays** buttons while it runs.

<div class="ar-demo" data-style="pop" data-chart="C|G|Am|F|C|G|F|C" data-tempo="70" data-comp="piano" data-on="comp" data-staves="comp bass"></div>

**Task.** Plan a four-step build for a three-verse ballad: who plays in verse 1, verse 2, the chorus, the last chorus? Write it as a table and keep it in your [process journal](process-journal.qmd).
A rule of thumb: **one new thing at each section**, never three.

## 2. Register: higher means more

When a melody or a piano part moves up, it sounds like more energy, more strain, more hope. The same chords an octave higher feel lighter; an octave lower, heavier.
Hear the piano in the same chords at three octaves (the first button is as written).

<div class="ar-demo" data-style="pop" data-chart="C|G|Am|F" data-tempo="72" data-comp="piano" data-choice-label="Piano:" data-choices='[{"label":"Middle","opts":{"octave":{"comp":0}}},{"label":"An octave up","opts":{"octave":{"comp":1}}},{"label":"An octave down","opts":{"octave":{"comp":-1}}}]'></div>

A common plan: verse low and close to speech, chorus higher. The melody's **climax** (see [Composing 1](compose-melody.qmd)) usually lands on the most important word of the story.

## 3. A chord that turns the mood: the borrowed minor iv

The song is in C major, so the F chord is the major IV. Change it to **F minor** (borrowed from C minor) and the same line suddenly sounds like it has had bad news.
Songwriters use it at the exact moment the story turns: *the good thing ends*. See [Borrowed Chords](borrowed-chords.qmd) for how it is built.

<div class="ar-demo" data-style="pop" data-chart="C|G|Am|F" data-tempo="72" data-comp="piano" data-choice-label="Last chord:" data-choices='[{"label":"F (major, the story is fine)","chart":"C|G|Am|F|C|G|Am|F"},{"label":"Fm (borrowed, something has gone wrong)","chart":"C|G|Am|F|C|G|Am|Fm"}]'></div>

Listen to the second time round. The only difference is one note in one chord, yet the mood shifts. Where in *your* story would you put it?

## 4. Not the ending you expected: the deceptive cadence

The strongest sense of an ending is **V to I** (G to C): the question is answered. If the music goes to **V then vi** (G to Am) instead, we arrive somewhere
close but sadder. It is the sound of "and yet". Use it when the story stops one step short of what the listener hoped for. (See [Cadences](cadences.qmd).)

<div class="ar-demo" data-style="pop" data-chart="C|F|G|C" data-tempo="72" data-comp="piano" data-choice-label="Ending:" data-choices='[{"label":"V to I (the answer)","chart":"C|F|G|C|C|F|G|C"},{"label":"V to vi (and yet)","chart":"C|F|G|C|C|F|G|Am"}]'></div>

## 5. Take everything away

The strongest line in many ballads is the one the band **leaves**. If the whole band is playing, the listener hears music; if only the voice is left, the listener hears a person.
The same idea is in [Fills, Riffs and Licks](fills-riffs.qmd): the band speaks in the gaps, and sometimes the most telling thing the band can do is not speak.

Hear a break: the band plays two bars, then bass and drums stop and only the piano is left.

<div class="ar-demo" data-style="pop" data-chart="C|G|Am|F|C|G|F|C" data-tempo="70" data-comp="piano" data-on="bass comp drums" data-staves="comp bass"></div>

Switch **Bass** and **Drums** off in the second half of the pass. Use the same trick before the last chorus: stop, leave one bar of silence, then start again with everyone.

## 6. Reading the toolbox in a real song

| Tool | What the listener feels | What to listen for |
|---|---|---|
| **Fewer players** | intimate, private | a voice and one instrument in verse 1 |
| **More players** | the stakes rise | a part joins at each new section |
| **Higher register** | more strain or hope | the chorus melody starts higher than the verse's |
| **Louder** | more urgency | the drums change from sticks to brushes, or the reverse |
| **A borrowed chord** | a shadow, a memory | one chord that sounds "off" for a moment |
| **A deceptive cadence** | a step short, or an unexpected turn | the line that should land on home goes somewhere else |
| **A key change** | a new level of feeling | the whole song lifts, often before the last chorus |
| **Silence or a stripped bar** | the line stands alone | the band stops before the most important word |

**Task.** Take the song in [Story Songs 1](story-songs.qmd#story-map-fill-it-in-while-you-listen) and add a fifth column to your map: *which of these tools does the music use here, and what does the story need at that point?*
